name: Spica
description: Two hot blue stars 77 parsecs away that circle each other every four days.

radius.source: Tkachenko et al. (2016), MNRAS 458, 1964, Table 7: primary radius 7.47 +/- 0.54 solar radii from the combined light- and radial-velocity-curve solution

mass.source: Tkachenko et al. (2016), MNRAS 458, 1964, Table 7: dynamical mass of the primary 11.43 +/- 1.15 solar masses

temperature.source: Tkachenko et al. (2016), MNRAS 458, 1964, Tables 4 and 7: primary Teff 25,300 +/- 500 K from the disentangled spectrum

radialVelocity.source: Tkachenko et al. (2016), MNRAS 458, 1964, Table 2: systemic velocity -0.5 +/- 1.1 km/s

distance.source: van Leeuwen (2007), A&A 474, 653, HIP 65474: Hipparcos parallax 13.06 +/- 0.70 mas, inverted

position.credit: Anderson & Francis (2012), Astronomy Letters 38, 331 (XHIP), Hipparcos astrometry

color.reason: Every spectrum of Spica is the blended light of both stars, the secondary giving 14.5 +/- 1.5% of it (Tkachenko et al. 2016, MNRAS 458, 1964, Table 4), so no archive spectrum is the primary's own

text.card: Two hot blue stars 77 parsecs away that circle each other every four days.
text.introduction: Their orbit weighs the larger at 11.43 solar masses: it is 7.47 solar radii, 25,300 K at its surface, and pulsates.

notes: Spica's orbit turns in its plane once every 139 years (Aufdenberg et al. 2007); it is drawn as the paper fixed it, at its 2007 epoch.
The position angle of the orbit's line of nodes on the sky is not measured; it is drawn at 0, a display convention.
